title: This mountain is our Ayodhya
hookLine: Rama walks Sita around the mountain and tells her he doesn't miss the kingdom at all
carry: dharma kept, the forest is home
tomorrow: why can't the old king sleep?
last: KEEP THE HOLY AT THE CENTER.

lines: EVERY HARD STORY HAS A PAUSE.
cards: Every hard story has a pause, a stretch where the characters simply get to live. On Chitrakuta, the exiles get theirs. The hut is built.
The days fall into a rhythm: bathing in the river, gathering fruit, sitting by the fire at night.
And one day Rama takes Sita by the hand and walks her around the mountain, pointing things out, the way you'd show someone a neighborhood you've just moved into and already love.

teach.h: I DON'T GRIEVE FOR THE KINGDOM.
teach.b: Look at the peaks, Rama tells Sita: some silver, some red, some gold, some the color of crystal. Look at the waterfalls, the flowering trees, the birds. Then he says something tender.
Seeing this mountain with you, I don't grieve for the kingdom. And he gives his reasons.
Living here brings him two good things: he keeps his father's word, and he gives his brother Bharata joy.

He takes her down to the Mandakini, where sages bathe with their arms raised to the sun and deer come down to drink. Think of this mountain as Ayodhya, he says, the deer as its people, the Mandakini as our own Sarayu.
Here's the teaching. Rama isn't at peace because the forest is pretty. He's at peace because he's doing his dharma, keeping the promise his father made, even at the cost of a crown.
That's why Hindus call him maryada purushottama, the best of people, who stays within the bounds of what's right. In the tradition, a word kept doesn't make the forest smaller. It makes it home.

Devotees often say his name with hers, Sita-Ram, the two together, as they are on this mountain. One honest note: Valmiki actually tells this scene a little later, while trouble is already on its way.

teach.h: DHARMA KEPT, THE FOREST IS HOME.
teach.b: We've placed it here because it's the clearest picture of those first days. Now back to Valmiki's order. Far away, the charioteer Sumantra is driving into Ayodhya with an empty chariot.
And an old king is waiting.

how: In the text, the Mandakini at Chitrakuta is where Rama and Sita bathe; pilgrims to Chitrakoot bathe in the same river today.

o: the mountain where the exiles find a happy pause in exile
the forest camp where the exiles stay only one night
the hill where Rama grieves daily for his lost kingdom

s: Rama spends the Chitrakoot days grieving for the kingdom
he tells Sita that on the mountain with her he doesn't grieve for it.
Rama names keeping his father's word as a reason he's content
the other is the joy it gives his brother Bharata.
Valmiki tells this scene exactly where we read it
he places it a little later, while trouble is on its way, for contrast.

games.q: a friend says Rama was a pushover for going quietly into an unfair exile. what fits today's teaching?
o: he should have fought for the crown.
he kept his father's word. for Hindus that's dharma, and it made the forest home.
he only went because he liked the forest.
games.why: Rama names his reasons: his father's word kept, and Bharata's joy. Hindus honor him as maryada purushottama for it.

practice: Many Hindus repeat Rama's name, often as Sita-Ram, as a quiet practice called japa. If you'd like, say it softly with your breath: Sita on the breath in, Ram on the breath out.
If you don't pray, bring to mind one promise you're keeping, even where it costs you, and let each breath out say: this is my part.

wordCard.voice: Chitrakoot, the happy pause. Rama keeps his father's word, and the mountain, with Sita beside him, becomes their Ayodhya.

orig.note: Sanskrit mandākinī: the river at Chitrakuta where Rama and Sita bathe; still the river of Chitrakoot town.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma kept, the forest is home. Rama lost a crown and kept his word. Day five hundred forty-one, done.
